items.summary: Full Waveform Inversion (FWI) is a fundamental inverse problem in geophysics to estimate subsurface properties, such as velocity, from seismic measurements. Recently, self-supervised learning methods remove the need for ground-truth velocity maps during training by leveraging a forward operator to simulate seismic data from predictions and backpropagate the gradients of reconstruction loss through it. In this work, we consider a more challenging setting without accessing such gradients. To this end, we incorporate reinforcement learning into self-supervised FWI and propose a framework named DeepWaveRL. Specifically, we reformulate FWI as a policy learning problem, where the policy network predicts velocity maps as actions, and a forward operator is used solely for simulation. A global scalar reward is computed based on data misfit for each prediction and used to weight policy gradients. Thus, learning proceeds without accessing the gradients from the forward operator. Given the indirect and coarse supervision signals, we further identify key strategies to stabilize learning and mitigate the spatial credit assignment bottleneck. Experimental results show that, despite relying entirely on a single scalar reward, DeepWaveRL achieves competitive performance compared to supervised and self-supervised baselines. These findings suggest that our framework offers a flexible and complementary learning paradigm for the FWI research community.
items.title: DeepWaveRL: Self-Supervised Full Waveform Inversion via Reinforcement Learning

items.summary: Prediction errors from video world models are often treated as physical surprise, but they can also reflect appearance, static content, motion, or ordinary prediction difficulty. We present an evaluation framework that separates what frozen representations contain, how they organize appearance and physical differences, and what changes a model's own prediction error. On IntPhys2, a benchmark of physically possible and impossible events, we compare representations from latent prediction, masked pixel reconstruction, and simple visual statistics. Appearance remains easy to decode, while V-JEPA2 exposes modest information about whether events are possible or impossible. Looking at the latent geometry, appearance changes become smaller compared with differences between videos, their directions line up more consistently across scenes, and their overlap with physical changes decreases in deeper layers. Across action-conditioned models, incorrect actions raise prediction error, while appearance changes also produce substantial responses. In Physion++ video clips, repeating a single frame can produce higher error than the original clip, while changing color throughout the clip can lower it. Using Kubric, a simulation and rendering framework, we find that impossible events can produce lower error than possible events. A fixed error threshold also incorrectly flags many possible events as impossible. A model can therefore represent physical information and respond to incorrect actions without its native prediction error reliably measuring physical surprise.
items.title: When Does Latent Prediction Error Support Physical Surprise Claims in Video World Models?

items.summary: Graph forecasters for sensor networks are trained in one regime and deployed in others, where sensor coupling and signal frequency content both change. We split this spectral shift into an operator channel and a frequency channel, each with a dimensionless measure. ST-GFM (Spectral-Temporal Graph Forecasting Model) filters every input step with Chebyshev and bidirectional diffusion filters on one learned, non-symmetric operator and alternates them with per-node temporal attention. For the operator channel we prove Frobenius-norm perturbation bounds for both graph branches, show that the Chebyshev bound is attained to first order, and compute its constant from the trained weights and the measured operator norm: 17.9 on METR-LA and 21.5 on PEMS-BAY. Under random edge dropout the trained layer moves by 2.0% to 3.1% of this bound. Masked Spectral Reconstruction (MSR), a self-supervised loss active in the first 40 epochs, matches the log power spectrum of the encoder output to that of the input. For small log-spectral residuals on unclamped bins it is proportional to an Itakura-Saito divergence to leading order. Removing it raises the 60-minute MAE by 0.30 on METR-LA, close to the 0.33 lost when all three self-supervised losses go. Under one shared evaluation pipeline, the 60-minute MAE of ST-GFM is 3.5% below a retrained STAEformer on METR-LA and 13.0% below it on PEMS-BAY. Its 60-minute MAE is 3.0980.017 on METR-LA (five seeds) and 1.5760.006 on PEMS-BAY (three seeds), the lowest PEMS-BAY MAE among twelve published baselines.
items.title: ST-GFM: Spectral-Temporal Graph Forecasting with Measured Perturbation Bounds and Masked Spectral Reconstruction

items.summary: Dataset description This dataset provides gap-filled daily, high-resolution binary snow cover maps for 12 eddy-covariance stations within the FLUXNET, ICOS, and i-Box networks distributed across the French, Swiss, Austrian, and Italian Alps. The maps were generated to characterize surface snow conditions within the source areas of eddy-covariance measurements for the updated analysis of Scheidt et al. (2026). The dataset was specifically used to determine whether the area enclosed by a station’s 80% flux-footprint contour was snow covered and to calculate the snow-cover fraction (SCF) within that footprint. Footprint-scale SCF can be calculated from the maps as the proportion of valid pixels within the footprint classified as snow covered. The data cover the following eddy-covariance sites for the hydrological years (1 st October - 30 th September) from 2013/14 to 2023/24: Alp Weissenstein (CH-Aws), Switzerland Col du Lautaret (FR-CLt), France Früebüel (CH-Fru), Switzerland Monte Bondone (IT-MBo), Italy Mazia Pasture (IT-MtP), Italy Neustift (AT-Neu), Austria Nivolet (IT-NiG), Italy Torgnon (IT-Tor), Italy The i-Box observational network in the Inn Valley, Austria, comprising the Eggen (CS-SF1), Kolsass (CS-VF0), Hochhäuser (CS-NF27), and Weerberg (CS-NF10) stations For each station outside the i-Box network, the NetCDF files cover a 15 km × 15 km square centered on the station. Because the four i-Box stations are located close to one another, they are represented by a common 20 km × 20 km domain centered on the station cluster. The maps have a spatial resolution of 50 m and are provided in the WGS 84 / UTM zone 32N coordinate reference system (EPSG:32632). Files are organized by site and hydrological year. The binary snow cover condition variable represents daily snow-cover conditions, while the reconstruction_method variable distinguishes pixels obtained from high-resolution satellite observations from pixels reconstructed by the gap-filling procedure. High-resolution snow cover fraction maps were derived from Sentinel-2 MSI and Landsat 8 and Landsat 9 OLI imagery using SnowFLAKES ( Snow extent from applying a Flexible Learning Algorithm using KErnel-based Spectral unmixing ) at a resolution of 50m. SnowFLAKES is an unsupervised, image-adaptive snow-mapping approach developed for mountainous terrain and challenging observation conditions, including topographic shadows and variable illumination. The processing follows the approach described by Barella et al. (2022). Daily, spatially complete maps were generated by combining the available high-resolution snow observations with daily, lower-resolution MODIS SCF from the MOD10A1 product (Hall and Riggs, 2021). Gap filling and spatial downscaling were performed using an implementation adapted from the hierarchical multiresolution data-fusion method proposed by Premier et al. (2021). The approach uses spatial patterns learned from available optical observations to reconstruct snow-cover conditions on days without usable high-resolution satellite imagery. The resulting product represents daily binary snow presence at high spatial resolution. Raw Sentinel-2, Landsat, and MODIS imagery, eddy-covariance measurements, and flux footprint polygons are not included in this archive. The archive also includes an interactive Python viewer for the daily *_SC_GAM.nc snow-cover products. It can display snow-cover classes and reconstruction provenance over time, with station locations shown for context. Setup instructions and examples are provided in the README. items.summary: Reduced-order models (ROMs) learned from trusted numerical simulations enable the real-time simulation of complex physical systems, making computationally prohibitive tasks-such as uncertainty quantification and optimal control-tractable. In particular, data-driven ROMs are opening the opportunity to learn from both numerical simulations and experimental data. However, integrating these sources of information is far from straightforward. Real-world measurements often involve multiple sources of uncertainty, including non-Gaussian noise, latent heterogeneities, unknown or hidden system parameters, and multiscale phenomena occurring below the resolution of the data. Consequently, real-world data are better described by parametrized stochastic partial differential equations, for which the development of effective ROMs remains relatively unexplored. In this work, we introduce POD-CNF, a data-driven generative ROM for efficient uncertainty quantification of parametrized high-dimensional systems. The approach combines projection-based model reduction and deep generative modeling. First, Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) is employed to obtain a low-dimensional representation of the solution manifold. A Conditional Normalizing Flow (CNF) is then trained to approximate the density of the reduced coefficients conditionally on the input parameters. This formulation allows the surrogate to capture complex, multimodal output distributions, going beyond standard regression-based ROMs and least-squares predictions. We assess the effectiveness of POD-CNF through numerical experiments, demonstrating its ability to accurately reproduce output distributions while substantially reducing computational costs. Finally, a proof-of-concept application illustrates how the generative paradigm facilitates integration into Bayesian inverse problems, highlighting promising directions for future research.
items.title: POD-CNF: reduced order modeling of parametrized stochastic PDEs via normalizing flows and proper orthogonal decomposition

items.summary: Scaling depth is a key route to stronger large language models, but Pre-LN architectures often suffer from depth-wise information dilution, limiting the effective use of deep layers. While cross-layer connectivity has proven effective at mitigating this problem, existing designs usually introduce additional computation or memory access. We revisit cross-layer KV sharing as an efficient form of such connectivity. Beyond cache compression, each KV reuse edge creates a direct gradient path from deep layers to source KV projections, turning KV sharing into an implicit structural regularizer for KV representation geometry. We provide a systematic analysis of this mechanism, showing that proper sharing topologies sharpen key retrieval directions while enriching the value content subspace, whereas existing adjacent or global-anchor designs do not fully exploit this effect. Motivated by this, we propose DepthGraft, a hierarchical KV-sharing architecture that reconstructs deep-layer KV from stride-aligned shallow-middle source pairs. DepthGraft distributes non-local gradient flow across source layers, while preserving prefill early completion and reducing KV cache by roughly one third. Experiments on dense and MoE models from 0.5B to 16B parameters show consistent downstream improvements under both GQA and MLA. Notably, on the 16B MoE model, DepthGraft achieves a 7.0% absolute improvement on MMLU-Pro, along with gains of 6.6% on CMMLU and 6.4% on C3. These results validate the potential of DepthGraft as a scalable design for large-scale pretraining. The project page is available at https://github.com/jianke0604/DepthGraft.
items.title: DepthGraft: Structural Regularization through Hierarchical Cross-Layer KV Reconstruction

items.summary: A causal video generator produces two key--value (KV) states for every segment: the KV it uses while denoising that segment, and the KV it writes into the cache for later segments to read. In a pretrained generator the two already differ substantially, later segments attend to them differently, and replacing the written KV with the generation KV degrades the continuation. We propose dKV Forcing (dKV denotes differentiable KV) to learn a dedicated memory representation from its future use: a writer-specific low-rank residual on the shared backbone separates memory writing from generation and is trained through the future reads of what it writes. Learning a write from its future use needs gradients through the cache, which the mutable cache in common use cannot provide. dKV Forcing replaces the training-time cache by persistent differentiable pages with local rematerialization and, in one temporal traversal, computes exactly the gradient that a two-pass reconstruction of the same objective computes. One traversal computes the full memory gradient at $7\%$ generator-update overhead over detached-write training, with $28\%$ less resident memory and $20.8\%$ shorter training cycles than the two-pass reconstruction. Over Self Gradient Forcing (SGF), the same objective trained with the same traversal, writer adaptation raises VBench-Long aesthetic quality by $6.6$ points at 60\,s and $8.5$ points at 240\,s with the highest subject and background consistency, and rollout dropout of the residual keeps most of this gain while restoring the motion of training without write gradients.
items.title: dKV Forcing: Separating Generation and Memory Representations through a Differentiable KV Cache

items.summary: We present Xiaomi Auto World Model 2.0, a unified streaming causal world model for Physical AI. It models and generates causal physical evolution in the real world, and unifies heterogeneous conditioning inputs for view-consistent generation. The architecture integrates View-Temporal Attention (VTA) to capture cross-view spatial dependencies and temporal dynamics, together with Multi-view Rotary Position Encoding (RoPE) to encode positional relationships across views and time. WorldRec 2.0 reconstructs static and dynamic 3D Gaussians from multi-view, multi-temporal observations in a single forward pass and uses their renderings as explicit scene context to preserve geometry and appearance during long-horizon generation. Conditioning inputs are fused through VAE latent concatenation in a shared representation space. We incorporate Gated Linear Attention (GLA) into the temporal layers of VTA for efficient streaming inference, reducing computation and KV-cache memory during multi-view rollouts. A physical-interaction data pipeline covers diverse interactions and long-tailed events. From Pre-train onward, these data are combined with large-scale videos and heterogeneous visual modalities to learn visual, geometric, and dynamic priors. During Mid-train, training across diverse view configurations further improves the model's ability to capture how actions and object states shape subsequent scene evolution. After distillation-based Post-train, we apply the model to closed-loop simulation, closed-loop training, and World Action Model (WAM) applications. These applications generate physically consistent future states and support world-state prediction, policy learning, and action generation for Physical AI.
items.title: Xiaomi Auto World Model 2.0: Causal World Models for Real-World Driving and Embodied Intelligence

items.summary: Abstract Sānér establishes a recursive control architecture for task regions by placing topology, self-modeling scheduling, and certificate-governed execution under one executable resource semantics. The nine-node construction supports exact recursive expansion and addressing. Its formal system establishes capacity safety, deterministic cross-layer selection, partition safety, conditional liveness, and computable deadline and recovery bounds. Using entity-isolated validation and one-time test splits, we evaluated the shared kernels and domain adapters in executable state-transition simulations and public benchmark workloads over 32–64 independent worlds, with deployment evidence obtained from 48 physical GPU blocks and eight fresh process pairs in the official Kubernetes scheduler-performance harness. Shared kernels with explicit domain realizations established task-level all-comparator superiority, while matched Kubernetes execution established a throughput advantage over the official default scheduler. The recursive representation preserved exact adjacency with a small measured footprint as graph size increased. Mechanism evidence remains separate from direct performance claims. Boundary results and nonidentifiability tests are reported independently. Together, the proofs and matched comparisons establish Sānér as a reusable and auditable control architecture whose shared mechanisms transfer across structurally different systems tasks. Validation design The study reports 52 simulation tasks and two deployment endpoints. Simulation comparisons use matched frozen worlds, observable information, action spaces, resource ceilings, and decision-time budgets. The Kubernetes deployment uses fresh paired processes under the same official scheduling and binding boundaries. Independent-unit inference, primary endpoints, and comparison procedures follow the recorded experimental contracts. Task-level all-comparator conclusions require passage against every member of the specified comparator family. Suite-defined Holm or FDR adjustments control multiplicity. Direct performance, mechanism validation, boundary results, and nonidentifiability remain separate evidence classes. Comparator strength and field standing Comparator selection was deliberately demanding. The experiments include established scheduling methods, matched MPC and CP-SAT, public MAPF implementations, official Kubernetes scheduling, strong decentralized-learning algorithms, and mature domain-specific methods. Every direct comparison uses matched information and resources. Executed comparator implementations are identified precisely. The consensus experiment uses a HotStuff three-chain simulation and a validation-tuned partition-threshold selector. The distribution-estimation experiment uses a discounted-loss context-depth KT mixture alongside Bayesian online changepoint prediction and discounted KT estimation. Published BFTBrain and context-tree weighting provide the corresponding methodological lineages. Results overview Sānér established task-level all-comparator superiority across 38 simulation tasks. Representative findings include a 764.53% improvement over equal-degree expander control, a 208.90% improvement over Exact Diffusion, and a 33.40% improvement over the Graph500 top-down port. At 5,000 nodes, the topology-based placement adapter sustained 69,258 placements per second. Under matched official Kubernetes execution, Sānér achieved 892.80 placements per second versus 371.19 for the default scheduler, with a mean paired throughput ratio of 2.40. items.summary: Classical creative-process orderings put divergence early and convergence late, and the Double Diamond formalises the rule twice over. This paper argues the ordering was never a law of cognition but a map of costs: divergence goes early because reopening a converged process has historically been ruinous, and the entire discipline of the framework exists to protect against that reopening. When drafting cost collapses by orders of magnitude, as it does when an author works with a language model as typewriter, the protected assumption dissolves and the optimal ordering inverts: converge first, then diverge, because a late horizon either restarts a now-cheap process or spawns a child concept from a sharpened parent. The paper's second claim types reviewer instances in multi-model chains by regression target rather than capability, and states the Hein Condition: a mode-regressing reviewer's yield is proportional to the sharpness of the artefact it receives, because the modal response to an unsharp artefact is the generic response, so the same instance is most fluent exactly where it is least useful. A slot theory follows, carnivore, auditor, mode-regressor, children, each reviewer placed where its failure mode is cheapest, and child viability rises with parent sharpness at spawn. The claims are exercised on a fully documented case: a five-pass, three-model review chain run on a single paper in a single day, with every absorption, declination, and provenance failure logged. Four predictions close, including that review chains are provenance systems measurable by the sibling paper's key-inflation ratio.

In one sentence: the matrix geometric mean can jump at singular matrices, every possible jump is described by one rank condition, and the same mechanism refutes a published claim that the symbol of the geometric mean of two GLT matrix-sequences is always the geometric mean of their symbols. The geometric mean A#B of two positive definite matrices is the matrix analogue of √(ab), used to average covariance matrices and structured matrices and to define the Matsumoto fidelity of quantum states. It need not be continuous at singular pairs. Theorem 1 shows that X is a limit of A j #B j with positive definite A j → A, B j → B exactly when X ≽ 0, the block matrix [[A, X], [X, B]] is positive semidefinite and its rank is at most the dimension N (a dilation description with an auxiliary contraction already follows from recent work of Jones; the explicit elimination is the contribution). At equal inputs this gives the full set of limits and the exact interval of limiting Matsumoto fidelities. For generalized locally Toeplitz (GLT) matrix-sequences, uniformly bounded positive definite inputs with identical scalar symbols can have geometric means with the wrong symbol (4/5 instead of 1 on half the interval) or no eigenvalue distribution at all. This refutes Theorem 4 and Conjecture 1 of the arXiv version of Ilyas, Khan, Loi and Serra-Capizzano and, according to an AI-assisted reading of the published text, Theorem 3 and Conjecture 1 of their article in Linear Algebra Appl. (2025); the failing step of the proof is located. Positive results: closure for every Kubo-Ando mean when the sum of the symbols is positive definite almost everywhere; a one-sided theorem that the regularised symbol is always an upper envelope; and, for bounded Riemann-integrable scalar symbols of the space variable only, a sharp dichotomy (the formula holds for every realisation if and only if the symbols have no common zero set of positive measure or essentially disjoint supports). The classical two-dimensional discontinuity, Ando's maximal characterisation and the envelope X ≼ A#B are earlier work and are credited. The archive contains the manuscript (PDF and Markdown source), two figures with the script that draws them, an exact verifier (verify_exact.py, Python standard library only, 1,030 rational and Gaussian-rational checks of closed forms and finite assemblies, with a mutation self-test) and its retained output, the bibliography with its Crossref/arXiv records, the dated novelty ledger, a revision note, CI and SHA-256 sums. Assurance: written proofs; the verifier checks finite exact identities, not the theorems' limits or quantifiers; internal AI-assisted review only (not human peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification). Creator: Anonymous. Text and figures CC0-1.0; code MIT.
items.title: Boundary limits of the matrix geometric mean and the failure of unrestricted GLT closure

items.summary: Action-conditioned world models are increasingly trained on data from randomized experiments, and whether their predictions respond to actions is usually checked by replacing or removing the actions and measuring the loss in accuracy. We show that such diagnostics report action effects where there are none: under autocorrelated designs, future actions stand in for history the model does not see, and a better model learns the stand-in better. When the design law is known, a conditional randomization test written as an e-value is valid in finite samples whatever the model, provided the resampler conditions on the full state the design used; resampling from a simpler law reproduces the false effect. We identify a second failure, specific to world models: when many sites share one action sequence (cells in a microscope field, pixels in a frame), the natural pooled score turns small model errors along the action contrast into overwhelming evidence against a true effect. In a pixel world, its median log e-value fell from $-17.3$ to $-6832$ as frames grew from 64 to 4096 pixels, while the oracle's rose. Tempering the score by a design effect estimated on training data changes the bet, not the validity. Our own preregistered analysis of optogenetic ERK experiments failed in exactly this way; a tempered statistic, selected on synthetic data and registered before the data were obtained, then rejected the null on a never-opened field ($E\approx 1.1\times10^{10}$). Every analysis is preregistered, fixed in a dated protocol before it was run, or labelled exploratory, and every reported result is generated from hashed result files.
items.title: Stand-In Effects and Pooling Amplification: Design-Based Tests of Whether Biological World Models Use Actions

items.summary: Sensor fusion, data fusion, dashboards and data visualisation are conventionally distinguished by input type and by where they sit in a processing stack. This paper argues that the distinction which matters for decision quality is a different one, and that it is two variables applied to all four: every representation of multi-source evidence collapses a distribution somewhere between sensor and decision, and representations differ in the locus of that collapse and in whether the residual uncertainty survives it as a carried object. Fusion collapses upstream and, when honest, ships the residual as covariance or hypothesis mass. Dashboards defer collapse to the viewer's retina and ship nothing; the resulting belief has no bookkeeping. Visualisation is the encoding of whichever object arrives, indifferent to whether it is a point or a distribution, which is why it is blamed for collapses committed upstream. The two variables, collapse locus and residual retention, place the four terms on one map, generalise the confabulation coefficient of The Confabulating Collator from language-model collators to the whole representation stack, and yield a diagnostic: the failure mode conventionally called bad fusion is a product that collapsed upstream and discarded its residual, delivering the confidence of a posterior with the epistemic hygiene of a gauge. The publicly reported expectation, in the investigation of the February 2026 Minab strike, that a targeting platform would have flagged contradictions it carried no representation of, is read as this failure at operational scale, with the causal question left where the public record leaves it. A design rule follows: defer collapse to the human where the human carries the prior the system lacks, fuse where they do not, and at neither locus discard the residual. The constructive requirement for language-level fusion products is stated and handed to a companion paper on divergence retention. The operator located in the architecture is Binary Bias.

items.summary: We introduce Synergetic Autonomous Intelligence (SAI), a theory and design program for learning systems that form, preserve, revise, and compose relations while continuing to learn. SAI is built on three axioms: consequential distinctions must not become orphaned (U); identity is determined by future-faithful continuation under a declared contract (I); and unresolved defects are repaired by the least lawful local completion at the lowest admitted grade (L). We model a model, agent, tool, team, or environment boundary as a recursive semi-closed system with a Kernel-Ring representation, a Compile-Open-Participate cycle, and a typed residual comparing actual with claimed continuation. Under explicit finite or affine contracts, we establish relative consistency and conditional non-redundancy of U/I/L, characterize a contract-relative semantic quotient, construct an exact joint stochastic refinement, derive a constrained residual contraction, prove finite-horizon continued-service viability, and give an executed-intervention identification result with an observational-confounding boundary. We define GRC-Close as the generative and repair schema for this contract. The framework also gives finite contracts for action-effect-feedback loop re-entry, partial failure, duplicate-effect idempotency, replay, concurrent delivery, causal uncertainty, and threshold-radix state representation. KREIT, the Kernel-Ring Equilibrium Information Theory layer, treats information as a typed, resource-bounded distinction; the control layer authorizes, executes, audits, and updates actions across cloud-edge-end scales. These results establish a common contract-level vocabulary for representation, relation, memory, action, communication, explanation, coordination, and growth, while marking the assumptions and open boundaries required for later generalization.
items.title: Synergetic Autonomous Intelligence: Three Axioms for Recursive Semi-Closed Learning

items.summary: Indirect prompt injection creates a distinctive risk for blue-team Large Language Model (LLM) agents in Security Operations Centers (SOCs). Malicious instructions can be embedded in telemetry, tickets, retrieval results, or memory and then propagate through alert triage, incident summarization, response recommendation, and Indicator of Compromise (IOC) extraction as locally plausible intermediate decisions. We characterize this failure mode as evidence-chain contamination of protected task state. The main challenge is task dependent: a suspicious string may be malicious control text for summarization but essential evidence for IOC extraction. To address this challenge, we propose StateFence, a task-aware evaluation and defense framework that treats severity labels, incident narratives, response policies, and IOC sets as protected states. StateFence maps indirect prompt-injection attacks into explicit, stealth, multi-hop, and persistent SOC evidence attacks, records observable propagation traces, and routes defenses according to the attacked state. Across controlled SOC cases and public-SOC validation cases, StateFence lowers attack success and reduces failures that appear only after evidence is poisoned, while preserving task utility and avoiding the indicator loss caused by task-mismatched filtering. Our findings indicate that robust blue-team LLM agents require mechanisms that preserve task-critical state under untrusted evidence.
items.title: StateFence: Task-State Protection Against Evidence-Chain Contamination in Blue-Team LLM Agents

items.summary: We present Xiaomi Auto World Model 2.0, a unified streaming causal world model for Physical AI. It models and generates causal physical evolution in the real world, and unifies heterogeneous conditioning inputs for view-consistent generation. The architecture integrates View-Temporal Attention (VTA) to capture cross-view spatial dependencies and temporal dynamics, together with Multi-view Rotary Position Encoding (RoPE) to encode positional relationships across views and time. WorldRec 2.0 reconstructs static and dynamic 3D Gaussians from multi-view, multi-temporal observations in a single forward pass and uses their renderings as explicit scene context to preserve geometry and appearance during long-horizon generation. Conditioning inputs are fused through VAE latent concatenation in a shared representation space. We incorporate Gated Linear Attention (GLA) into the temporal layers of VTA for efficient streaming inference, reducing computation and KV-cache memory during multi-view rollouts. A physical-interaction data pipeline covers diverse interactions and long-tailed events. From Pre-train onward, these data are combined with large-scale videos and heterogeneous visual modalities to learn visual, geometric, and dynamic priors. During Mid-train, training across diverse view configurations further improves the model's ability to capture how actions and object states shape subsequent scene evolution. After distillation-based Post-train, we apply the model to closed-loop simulation, closed-loop training, and World Action Model (WAM) applications. These applications generate physically consistent future states and support world-state prediction, policy learning, and action generation for Physical AI.
items.title: Xiaomi Auto World Model 2.0: Causal World Models for Real-World Driving and Embodied Intelligence

items.summary: Memory systems for LLM agents are evaluated mostly on social dialogue, where facts accumulate and rarely change, so remembering reduces largely to finding the turn in which something was said. Financial dialogue breaks this assumption: figures are revised, stances shift without being restated, rules stated once govern later questions, and a single company is discussed under several analytical lenses. Memory systems that retrieve the passages most similar to a question, or the most recent ones, therefore return superseded values, miss rules that share no wording with the question, and cannot recover a stance spread across sessions. We present TrackMem, a per-speaker graph memory that tracks the history of figures, separates perspectives by entity and lens, and preserves each speaker's actions in chronological order. To evaluate it, we introduce FinLoCoMo, a benchmark of 15 long-horizon investment conversations with 765 questions in two splits: one following the LoCoMo categories and one targeting four failure modes. With two readers, TrackMem outperforms existing memory systems on both splits. On the failure-mode split it reaches 73.9% macro accuracy against 69.4% for the strongest baseline, with the largest gains on questions about revised figures (86.5% against 73.4%).
items.title: TrackMem: Tracking Evolving Beliefs in Long-Horizon Financial Dialogue

items.summary: Optimal control of partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs), in general, requires a complete history. The belief state, a distribution over hidden states, summarizes this history and provides the classical sufficient statistic to control POMDPs. However, the continuous nature of the belief space generally prevents a finite-memory controller from maintaining it exactly. This raises the question we address in this work: what must the available finite memory preserve to achieve near-optimal control performance? We study this question through an information-theoretic converse that gives a fundamental lower bound on the loss of any finite-memory controller. The analysis introduces the concept of a decision witness that characterizes belief states whose confusion would lead to unavoidable loss. Motivated by this bound, we propose RECAP, a constructive quantization method for designing representative memory states. We prove an upper bound on the optimality gap of any RECAP codebook and use the components of this bound together with the converse analysis to define the codebook objective. Experiments on 11 POMDP benchmarks demonstrate that RECAP improves over finite-memory representation baselines under the same memory budget.
items.title: Finite-Memory Control of POMDPs: Fundamental Limits and Efficient Design

items.summary: Visual mental imagery (VMI) decoding uses brain activity to reconstruct internally generated visual scenes, providing a potential pathway for externalizing internal experiences and developing neuroprosthetic communication interfaces. However, progress is limited by the lack of dedicated, training-scale VMI datasets. Current VMI paradigms often rely on visual prompts or short-term memory images, introducing visual and mnemonic confounds that make it difficult to disentangle neural activity associated with endogenous image construction from signals driven by prior or concurrent visual input. items.summary: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization has emerged as a promising approach for memory-efficient large language model (LLM) post-training, yet its reliable application to reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) remains largely unexplored. Motivated by the distinct data regimes of on-policy RL and fixed-data optimization, we develop a generic variance-theoretic framework to investigate what limits the reliability of ZO gradient estimation. Our analysis reveals that estimation reliability is structurally determined by whether the two finite-difference evaluations are performed on matched data. Controlled perturbation-scale sweeps and matched-versus-mismatched end-to-end comparisons validate the predicted effect of data matching. Experiments across three model variants and two mathematical reasoning benchmarks further show that ZO-BOLT consistently improves over the pretrained baseline while retaining a near-inference memory footprint. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/lianmin-chen/the_cost_of_mismatch.

items.summary: Abstract Sānér establishes a recursive control architecture for task regions by placing topology, self-modeling scheduling, and certificate-governed execution under one executable resource semantics. The nine-node construction supports exact recursive expansion and addressing. Its formal system establishes capacity safety, deterministic cross-layer selection, partition safety, conditional liveness, and computable deadline and recovery bounds. Using entity-isolated validation and one-time test splits, we evaluated the shared kernels and domain adapters in executable state-transition simulations and public benchmark workloads over 32–64 independent worlds, with deployment evidence obtained from 48 physical GPU blocks and eight fresh process pairs in the official Kubernetes scheduler-performance harness. Shared kernels with explicit domain realizations established task-level all-comparator superiority, while matched Kubernetes execution established a throughput advantage over the official default scheduler. The recursive representation preserved exact adjacency with a small measured footprint as graph size increased. Mechanism evidence remains separate from direct performance claims. Boundary results and nonidentifiability tests are reported independently. Together, the proofs and matched comparisons establish Sānér as a reusable and auditable control architecture whose shared mechanisms transfer across structurally different systems tasks. Validation design The study reports 52 simulation tasks and two deployment endpoints. Simulation comparisons use matched frozen worlds, observable information, action spaces, resource ceilings, and decision-time budgets. The Kubernetes deployment uses fresh paired processes under the same official scheduling and binding boundaries. Independent-unit inference, primary endpoints, and comparison procedures follow the recorded experimental contracts. Task-level all-comparator conclusions require passage against every member of the specified comparator family. Suite-defined Holm or FDR adjustments control multiplicity. Direct performance, mechanism validation, boundary results, and nonidentifiability remain separate evidence classes. Comparator strength and field standing Comparator selection was deliberately demanding. The experiments include established scheduling methods, matched MPC and CP-SAT, public MAPF implementations, official Kubernetes scheduling, strong decentralized-learning algorithms, and mature domain-specific methods. Every direct comparison uses matched information and resources. Executed comparator implementations are identified precisely. The consensus experiment uses a HotStuff three-chain simulation and a validation-tuned partition-threshold selector. The distribution-estimation experiment uses a discounted-loss context-depth KT mixture alongside Bayesian online changepoint prediction and discounted KT estimation. Published BFTBrain and context-tree weighting provide the corresponding methodological lineages. Results overview Sānér established task-level all-comparator superiority across 38 simulation tasks. Representative findings include a 764.53% improvement over equal-degree expander control, a 208.90% improvement over Exact Diffusion, and a 33.40% improvement over the Graph500 top-down port. At 5,000 nodes, the topology-based placement adapter sustained 69,258 placements per second. Under matched official Kubernetes execution, Sānér achieved 892.80 placements per second versus 371.19 for the default scheduler, with a mean paired throughput ratio of 2.40. Exact recursive-topology representation preserved neighbor recovery at 508–716 measured bytes through 26,244 nodes. Complete self-modeling was measured independently. items.summary: Optimal control of partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs), in general, requires a complete history. The belief state, a distribution over hidden states, summarizes this history and provides the classical sufficient statistic to control POMDPs. However, the continuous nature of the belief space generally prevents a finite-memory controller from maintaining it exactly. This raises the question we address in this work: what must the available finite memory preserve to achieve near-optimal control performance? We study this question through an information-theoretic converse that gives a fundamental lower bound on the loss of any finite-memory controller. The analysis introduces the concept of a decision witness that characterizes belief states whose confusion would lead to unavoidable loss. Motivated by this bound, we propose RECAP, a constructive quantization method for designing representative memory states. We prove an upper bound on the optimality gap of any RECAP codebook and use the components of this bound together with the converse analysis to define the codebook objective. Experiments on 11 POMDP benchmarks demonstrate that RECAP improves over finite-memory representation baselines under the same memory budget.
items.title: Finite-Memory Control of POMDPs: Fundamental Limits and Efficient Design

items.summary: An AI can find a safe action faster than any human, but it must never decide what counts as safe. We present GURU, a hierarchical neuro-symbolic multi-agent system for mission-critical digital engineering and operations, built on one partition of authority: learned models propose, rank, and accelerate; a symbolic rules engine checks every consequential action against hard limits before it executes; and validated physics confirms and decides. GURU runs a workflow as a closed control loop, with Navigation, Action, and Planning agents sharing one Common Internal Language and one training factory. Nuclear, aviation, and national-security guidance now requires this pattern; a harnessed language model keeps the model at the center, GURU puts a validated reference there. In computational fluid dynamics, the workflow raised the converged-simulation rate on unseen aircraft geometries from under 1 percent to 74 percent over 100 single-attempt cases, ran 54 live cases to Mach 6 on three facilities, and an ablation put the symbolic layer at 13 points of boundary-layer capture. Knowledge-graph retrieval and role adapters raised ParaView control success from 55 to 75 percent. In space domain awareness, where a language model cannot be trusted to decide, a frozen self-supervised world model under validated propagation scored highest of five methods at conjunction risk, including fully fine-tuned language models, with several-times-lower seed variance: the trustworthy design gives up nothing in accuracy, and the recipe transferred to reactor anomaly detection. A radar-to-avoidance debris pipeline was demonstrated in stages on a 2026 reentry; the hierarchy coordinates simulated teams of 200 aircraft. Training scaled near-linearly past 1,000 Aurora nodes and ran at 8,000. The approach extends to a control-grade microreactor digital twin with validated physics, not a learned model, as the safety basis.
items.title: GURU: A Hierarchical Neuro-Symbolic Multi-Agent System for Verification-Aware Automation of Mission-Critical Digital Engineering and Operations

items.summary: Prediction errors from video world models are often treated as physical surprise, but they can also reflect appearance, static content, motion, or ordinary prediction difficulty. We present an evaluation framework that separates what frozen representations contain, how they organize appearance and physical differences, and what changes a model's own prediction error. On IntPhys2, a benchmark of physically possible and impossible events, we compare representations from latent prediction, masked pixel reconstruction, and simple visual statistics. Appearance remains easy to decode, while V-JEPA2 exposes modest information about whether events are possible or impossible. Looking at the latent geometry, appearance changes become smaller compared with differences between videos, their directions line up more consistently across scenes, and their overlap with physical changes decreases in deeper layers. Across action-conditioned models, incorrect actions raise prediction error, while appearance changes also produce substantial responses. In Physion++ video clips, repeating a single frame can produce higher error than the original clip, while changing color throughout the clip can lower it. Using Kubric, a simulation and rendering framework, we find that impossible events can produce lower error than possible events. A fixed error threshold also incorrectly flags many possible events as impossible. A model can therefore represent physical information and respond to incorrect actions without its native prediction error reliably measuring physical surprise.
items.title: When Does Latent Prediction Error Support Physical Surprise Claims in Video World Models?

items.summary: Language models in customer-facing products must be continually updated, since the data they serve shifts over time. As retraining on the full accumulated data is impractical, each update should instead run on a small set of examples carrying the training signal of all data seen so far. The strongest current methods build this set by gradient matching, which synthesizes examples whose training gradients match those of the full data. However, they require ground-truth labels, run once on a fixed snapshot rather than on a growing stream, and are slow on large data. We introduce \textbf{OLGA}, which lifts these limitations. It distills unlabeled data by drawing the gradient matching targets from the model's own next-token predictions. Across five text classification benchmarks with phi-1.5, it improves accuracy by 10 percentage points over the strongest selection baseline using as few as five examples. OLGA also distills online data streams by keeping a running rehearsal memory of synthetic examples, which is re-distilled together with each new batch as it arrives. In the online setting, it outperforms the strongest selection-based continual baseline by 6.6 stream-AUC percentage points. Finally, our method scales to large data by pairing distillation with selection in a hybrid pipeline, letting selection handle the mild stage of compression and distillation the extreme one. It cuts runtime by 30\% versus distillation alone at similar accuracy, and beats the best selection-only pipeline by up to 12.6 percentage points.
items.title: Online Label-Free Gradient Matching for Continual Language Model Training

items.summary: Memory systems for LLM agents are evaluated mostly on social dialogue, where facts accumulate and rarely change, so remembering reduces largely to finding the turn in which something was said. Financial dialogue breaks this assumption: figures are revised, stances shift without being restated, rules stated once govern later questions, and a single company is discussed under several analytical lenses. Memory systems that retrieve the passages most similar to a question, or the most recent ones, therefore return superseded values, miss rules that share no wording with the question, and cannot recover a stance spread across sessions. We present TrackMem, a per-speaker graph memory that tracks the history of figures, separates perspectives by entity and lens, and preserves each speaker's actions in chronological order. To evaluate it, we introduce FinLoCoMo, a benchmark of 15 long-horizon investment conversations with 765 questions in two splits: one following the LoCoMo categories and one targeting four failure modes. With two readers, TrackMem outperforms existing memory systems on both splits. On the failure-mode split it reaches 73.9% macro accuracy against 69.4% for the strongest baseline, with the largest gains on questions about revised figures (86.5% against 73.4%).
items.title: TrackMem: Tracking Evolving Beliefs in Long-Horizon Financial Dialogue

items.summary: Long-horizon tasks require large language model (LLM) agents to coordinate interdependent actions, a capability central to automating complex workflows. Stepwise group-based reinforcement learning provides finer credit than trajectory-level supervision, but reliable comparisons must account for differences in interaction history. Enforcing this consistency within the limited rollouts of each task can leave insufficient support for estimating action preferences. We propose Beyond-Local Policy Optimization (BLPO), which estimates task-progress advantages from experience shared across tasks and training updates. We summarize trajectory prefixes into task-progress states and abstract actions by their function, allowing corresponding decisions from different tasks to contribute to shared estimates. To control bias and noise from heterogeneous tasks, we accumulate context-relative returns in a global memory with balanced aggregation and reliability weighting. These global advantages complement local comparisons over normalized actions and trajectory-level credit without a learned critic or additional rollouts. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop with 1.5B and 7B policies show improved task success over the evaluated baselines under matched training budgets. Further analyses show faster learning and shorter trajectories with little computational overhead.
items.title: BLPO: Beyond-Local Policy Optimization for Long-Horizon LLM Agents

items.summary: Full Waveform Inversion (FWI) is a fundamental inverse problem in geophysics to estimate subsurface properties, such as velocity, from seismic measurements. Recently, self-supervised learning methods remove the need for ground-truth velocity maps during training by leveraging a forward operator to simulate seismic data from predictions and backpropagate the gradients of reconstruction loss through it. In this work, we consider a more challenging setting without accessing such gradients. To this end, we incorporate reinforcement learning into self-supervised FWI and propose a framework named DeepWaveRL. Specifically, we reformulate FWI as a policy learning problem, where the policy network predicts velocity maps as actions, and a forward operator is used solely for simulation. A global scalar reward is computed based on data misfit for each prediction and used to weight policy gradients. Thus, learning proceeds without accessing the gradients from the forward operator. Given the indirect and coarse supervision signals, we further identify key strategies to stabilize learning and mitigate the spatial credit assignment bottleneck. Experimental results show that, despite relying entirely on a single scalar reward, DeepWaveRL achieves competitive performance compared to supervised and self-supervised baselines. These findings suggest that our framework offers a flexible and complementary learning paradigm for the FWI research community.
items.title: DeepWaveRL: Self-Supervised Full Waveform Inversion via Reinforcement Learning

items.summary: Deep learning models for electronic health records achieve strong predictive performance but provide little insight into what clinical concepts they represent internally. Post-hoc attribution methods produce per-cell importance scores that lack temporal coherence, cross-variable structure, and reusability across patients. We introduce the Temporal Island Sparse Autoencoder (TI-SAE), which learns a backbone-specific, patient-shared clinical concept dictionary from a frozen predictive model's representations. Each dictionary entry (latent) is defined by learned temporal Gaussian islands (specifying when the concept is active) and a sparse variable-composition vector (specifying which variables are involved). A decoupled selector then identifies which dictionary entries drive each patient's prediction, separating representation learning from attribution. We evaluate TI-SAE across five backbone architectures spanning different representation strategies on MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV (three prediction tasks each). TI-SAE produces structured clinical concepts that go beyond transient attribution heatmaps while achieving strong performance on standard faithfulness benchmarks.
items.title: Temporal Island Sparse Autoencoders for Interpreting Clinical Time-Series Models

items.summary: Reduced-order models (ROMs) learned from trusted numerical simulations enable the real-time simulation of complex physical systems, making computationally prohibitive tasks-such as uncertainty quantification and optimal control-tractable. In particular, data-driven ROMs are opening the opportunity to learn from both numerical simulations and experimental data. However, integrating these sources of information is far from straightforward. Real-world measurements often involve multiple sources of uncertainty, including non-Gaussian noise, latent heterogeneities, unknown or hidden system parameters, and multiscale phenomena occurring below the resolution of the data. Consequently, real-world data are better described by parametrized stochastic partial differential equations, for which the development of effective ROMs remains relatively unexplored. In this work, we introduce POD-CNF, a data-driven generative ROM for efficient uncertainty quantification of parametrized high-dimensional systems. The approach combines projection-based model reduction and deep generative modeling. First, Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) is employed to obtain a low-dimensional representation of the solution manifold. A Conditional Normalizing Flow (CNF) is then trained to approximate the density of the reduced coefficients conditionally on the input parameters. This formulation allows the surrogate to capture complex, multimodal output distributions, going beyond standard regression-based ROMs and least-squares predictions. We assess the effectiveness of POD-CNF through numerical experiments, demonstrating its ability to accurately reproduce output distributions while substantially reducing computational costs. Finally, a proof-of-concept application illustrates how the generative paradigm facilitates integration into Bayesian inverse problems, highlighting promising directions for future research.
items.title: POD-CNF: reduced order modeling of parametrized stochastic PDEs via normalizing flows and proper orthogonal decomposition

items.summary: The feasibility of updating and synchronising digital twins of actuated systems from operational data depends strongly on how the system is controlled and, consequently, on the data generated during operation. This establishes a direct link between control actuation and model identifiability. This work presents a reinforcement-twinning framework that exploits this link through three computational components. A Gaussian-process surrogate of the physical return combines the twin prediction, used as a calibrated trend, with a discrepancy learned from measured returns, allowing Bayesian policy search to exploit the twin without being tied to its predictions. Candidate policies are proposed around the policy that is optimal for the twin, while measured returns can expand this region. The resulting physical episodes are replayed on the twin after observer-based synchronisation with sparse measurements, and its parameters are identified by combining Bayesian optimisation with gradient-based refinement. Selected information-oriented episodes deploy an excitation policy to improve parameter identifiability. The framework is demonstrated on a Burgers-flow analogue of dynamic-induction control in wind farms, with a deliberately misspecified model structure. Despite substantially biased return predictions, the twin provides a useful starting policy and search region, placing the guided search ahead of unguided Bayesian optimisation from its first physical evaluations. This advantage is maintained when the search region is allowed to expand in response to changes in measured returns, whereas searches over-constrained by the twin-defined region are eventually overtaken by the unguided alternatives. The results support reinforcement twinning as a framework for jointly adapting models and control policies when physical interaction is limited and model discrepancy cannot be neglected.
items.title: Reinforcement Twinning via Twin-Calibrated Bayesian Policy Search and Replay-Driven Identification

items.summary: The self-controlled case series (SCCS) design is widely used in studies of rare events, for example of vaccine side effects. Conceptually, the design has two main features. First, it requires only data from individuals who have experienced the event of interest. Therefore, the design is especially useful when the outcome is rare and the available data come from surveillance or clinical records, say, of hospitalized patients. Second, because comparisons are made within single individuals, time-invariant confounding between treatment and outcome is eliminated. We formulate a set of sufficient identification assumptions for estimating the causal effect of vaccination on an adverse outcome under the SCCS design, drawing on ideas from the causal inference literature. Unlike the existing SCCS literature, we do not consider a parametric model as the starting point. This allows us to establish when and why the SCCS design allows identification of causal effects, using data from cases only. However, because the sufficient identifiability assumptions are implausible in some applications, we also develop statistical tests for the existence of a treatment effect that remain valid when only a subset of the identification assumptions holds.
items.title: Causal Inference from Self-controlled Case Series

items.summary: Graph forecasters for sensor networks are trained in one regime and deployed in others, where sensor coupling and signal frequency content both change. We split this spectral shift into an operator channel and a frequency channel, each with a dimensionless measure. ST-GFM (Spectral-Temporal Graph Forecasting Model) filters every input step with Chebyshev and bidirectional diffusion filters on one learned, non-symmetric operator and alternates them with per-node temporal attention. For the operator channel we prove Frobenius-norm perturbation bounds for both graph branches, show that the Chebyshev bound is attained to first order, and compute its constant from the trained weights and the measured operator norm: 17.9 on METR-LA and 21.5 on PEMS-BAY. Under random edge dropout the trained layer moves by 2.0% to 3.1% of this bound. Masked Spectral Reconstruction (MSR), a self-supervised loss active in the first 40 epochs, matches the log power spectrum of the encoder output to that of the input. For small log-spectral residuals on unclamped bins it is proportional to an Itakura-Saito divergence to leading order. Removing it raises the 60-minute MAE by 0.30 on METR-LA, close to the 0.33 lost when all three self-supervised losses go. Under one shared evaluation pipeline, the 60-minute MAE of ST-GFM is 3.5% below a retrained STAEformer on METR-LA and 13.0% below it on PEMS-BAY. Its 60-minute MAE is 3.0980.017 on METR-LA (five seeds) and 1.5760.006 on PEMS-BAY (three seeds), the lowest PEMS-BAY MAE among twelve published baselines.
items.title: ST-GFM: Spectral-Temporal Graph Forecasting with Measured Perturbation Bounds and Masked Spectral Reconstruction

items.summary: Version 1.02, 3 November 2026. Acemoglu and Restrepo (2020) estimate that one additional industrial robot per thousand workers lowers a U.S. local labor market's employment-to-population ratio by 0.39 percentage points and its hourly wages by about 0.77 percent. Rebuilding their design from raw IPUMS, IFR, and EU KLEMS data, I reproduce these estimates bit-exactly. I then ask what conventional robustness checks leave open: which industries, places, periods, and shocks actually identify the estimate? The regression spans 722 commuting zones and 19 industries, but the variation behind an instrumental-variable estimate can be far narrower. The sign is robust; the support is narrow. Negative estimates persist across conventional specification changes, 60 strong European instrument windows, alternative U.S. treatment windows, and the published periods through 2014. Yet automotive carries about 84 percent of normalized absolute Rotemberg-weight mass, and automotive exposure in six Rust Belt states supplies 95 percent of the net first-stage covariance. Without automotive, the remaining 18 industry shocks do not strongly predict U.S. robot exposure. Longer horizons, later start years, and adding Germany to the instrument all strengthen it through the same margin. The automotive component shows no detectable relation to 1970–1990 employment and wage changes, and a direct effect of the instrument would have to absorb 72 percent of the reduced form before conventional significance disappears. Inference is weaker than the regional first stage suggests. With 19 underlying industry shocks, exposure-robust first-stage F-statistics are 6.2 and 6.3 rather than 34, small-sample Anderson–Rubin tests do not reject a zero effect ( p = 0.059, 0.063), and other implementations of the same test disagree; in known-truth simulations, nominal 95-percent state-clustered intervals cover in only 60–66 percent of replications. Measurement assumptions also bind. In the original penetration metric, perpetual-inventory robot capital preserves the estimates at 5 percent depreciation, but faster assumed depreciation counts the automotive installations behind the first stage as replacement rather than net additions, eliminating shock-level relevance at 10 percent and all relevance at 15 percent. The benchmark is reproducible and robust in sign, but it is identified from an automotive margin in historically industrial labor markets; that margin defines its scope and the concrete content of its exclusion restriction. More generally, coefficient robustness and breadth of identifying support are distinct properties that shift-share studies should report separately.
